# Volume 3 — Chapter XII “Evadne’s Atonement”

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

“What are you daydreaming about, Nell?”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0000 }

One dusk, the pair of young females was lingering beside a enchanted glen belonging to the stream. Within it, fronds dipped, and tiny blades of turf showed vivid green, while wild pear trees draped sweetly-fragranced, pale drapes about the spot.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0001 }

With a contented sigh, Nell shook off her daydreaming.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0002 }

“I was developing my tale in my mind, Isolde.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0003 }

“Oh, is it true that you’ve started it?” Isolde exclaimed, instantly glowing with enthusiastic curiosity.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0004 }

“Yes, I have composed merely a couple of pages, yet the whole thing is mapped out quite thoroughly in my mind. Finding an appropriate plot has been an enormous struggle for me. Every single plot I came up with seemed ill-fitted for a girl called Evadne.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0005 }

“Was it not possible for you to have given her a different name?”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0006 }

“No, it was an impossible thing. Although I attempted to, I was unable to accomplish it, just as I could not alter yours. Evadne possessed such reality for me that regardless of any alternative name I attempted to assign to her, I simply considered her to be Evadne beneath everything. Eventually, however, I obtained a storyline that suited her. After that, the thrill of selecting names for every one of my characters arrived. How captivating that process is, you cannot imagine. For hours I have stayed awake contemplating those names. Perceval Dalrymple is the name of the hero.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0007 }

“Are all the characters named by you?” Isolde inquired longing. “I was planning to request that you allow me to give a name to one if you hadn’t—simply an insignificant individual. It would make me feel like I possessed a part of the tale in that case.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0008 }

“The small hired lad residing alongside the Lesters can be named by you,” Nell granted. “While his significance is minimal, no one else remains without a name.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0009 }

“Name him Raymond Fitzosborne,” Isolde proposed, as she possessed a supply of those names stored in her mind, remnants from the former “Story Club,” an association that she, Nell, Odette Pullen, and Opal Pettigrew had kept during their school years.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0010 }

With a shake of her head, Nell expressed her doubt.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0011 }

“I fear such a name possesses too much nobility for a farmhand, Isolde. Could you envision a Fitzosborne tending to swine and gathering kindling?”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0012 }

If one possessed any imagination whatsoever, Isolde failed to understand why it could not be expanded to such a degree; yet Nell likely possessed superior judgment, and ultimately the chore boy was named Robert Ray, with the option of being referred to as Bobby if the situation demanded it.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0013 }

“What amount do you think you’ll receive for it?” Isolde inquired.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0014 }

However, this had not crossed Nell’s mind whatsoever. Her quest was for renown rather than vile money, and financial motives had not yet corrupted her writerly ambitions.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0015 }

“Won’t you permit me to read it?” begged Isolde.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0016 }

“Once it is completed, I will share it with you and Mr. Pettifer by reading it aloud, and I will require your rigorous critique. Before its publication, no other person will be permitted to view it.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0017 }

“In what manner will you conclude it—with a happy ending or an unhappy one?”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0018 }

“I am uncertain. Ending it unhappily is my preference, since that would be far more romantic. However, I am aware that editors are prejudiced against tragic conclusions. I once overheard Professor Hamilton remark that writing a sad ending should only be attempted by a genius. And,” Nell added with modesty, “a genius is the last thing I am.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0019 }

“Oh, happy endings are my favourite. Allowing him to wed her would be best,” uttered Isolde, who believed that all tales ought to conclude in this manner, particularly after becoming betrothed to Gideon.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0020 }

“Yet you enjoy weeping when tales are told?”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0021 }

“Oh, yes, right in the center of them. However, I prefer for all things to end well eventually.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0022 }

“There has to be a single touching scene included,” Nell remarked in a reflective manner. “It’s possible I could cause Robert Ray to get hurt in a mishap and incorporate a deathbed scene.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0023 }

“No, Bobby must not be killed off,” Isolde declared, with a laugh. “I claim him, so it is my wish for him to stay alive and thrive. If a character must die, let it be another.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0024 }

During the following two weeks, Nell suffered or delighted, depending on her frame of mind, in her writing endeavors. At times she became overjoyed by a fantastic notion, and at other times she felt hopeless when a stubborn character refused to conduct themselves correctly. Isolde was unable to comprehend this.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0025 }

“Force them to act according to your desires,” she said.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0026 }

“I am unable to,” Nell lamented. “Evadne proves to be a heroine who is so difficult to control. She persists in acting and speaking in ways I did not intend for her. Subsequently, that ruins all the preceding material, forcing me to rewrite the entire thing.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0027 }

At last, nevertheless, the tale reached its completion, and Nell recited it to Isolde within the privacy of the porch gable. She had managed to include her “pathetic scene” while keeping Robert Ray alive, and she observed Isolde attentively throughout her reading. Isolde met her expectations by weeping appropriately; yet, as the conclusion arrived, she appeared somewhat dissatisfied.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0028 }

“What made you murder Marcel Lennox?” she inquired in a tone of blame.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0029 }

“The villain was who he was,” Nell argued. “Punishment had to be given to him.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0030 }

“Of everyone, he is my favorite,” declared irrational Isolde.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0031 }

“Indeed, he is deceased, and he must remain so,” Nell remarked, with a touch of resentment. “Had I allowed him to survive, he would have continued his harassment of Evadne and Perceval.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0032 }

“Yes—unless he had been reformed by you.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0033 }

“It wouldn’t have been romantic, and, what’s more, the story would have been made too long.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0034 }

“At any rate, it is a thoroughly delightful tale, Nell, and I am certain it will bring you fame. Have you thought of a name for it?”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0035 }

“Oh, the title was chosen by me a long time back. Evadne’s atonement is what I name it. Isn't that pleasing and alliterative in sound? Now, Isolde, speak to me honestly, are there any flaws you perceive in my tale?”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0036 }

“Well,” Isolde wavered, “the section in which Evadne bakes the cake appears to my mind not entirely romantic enough for the remainder. Anyone could do precisely that. I am of the opinion that heroines ought not to engage in cooking.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0037 }

“Why, that is the source of the humor, and it represents one of the finest elements of the entire tale,” Nell stated. And it can be affirmed that regarding this point she was entirely correct.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0038 }

Isolde wisely held back from making any additional critiques, though Mr. Pettifer proved far more difficult to satisfy. To begin with, he informed her that the narrative contained far too much description.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0039 }

“Omit all those ornate sections,” he stated callously.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0040 }

Nell possessed an uneasy belief that Mr. Pettifer was correct, and she compelled herself to remove the majority of her cherished descriptions, even though the tale required three rewrites until it could be trimmed sufficiently to satisfy the exacting Mr. Pettifer.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0041 }

“Except for the sunset, I have omitted every description,” she finally remarked. “It was impossible for me to part with it. None of the others were as good.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0042 }

“It is completely unrelated to the tale,” Mr. Pettifer said, “and you ought not to have set the action amidst wealthy city folk. What acquaintance do you have with such individuals? Why did you not set it directly here in Brierley—altering the name, naturally, or otherwise Mrs. Agatha Sowerby would likely imagine herself to be the main character.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0043 }

“Oh, such an idea would not have worked at all,” Nell objected. “Although Brierley is the most cherished location on earth, it lacks sufficient romance to serve as a tale's setting.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0044 }

“I imagine quite a few romances have occurred in Brierley—along with quite a few tragedies as well,” Mr. Pettifer observed dryly. “However, the people you write about are unlike actual people in any location. Their speech is overly abundant, and they employ excessively elaborate phrasing. In one particular spot, that Dalrymple fellow speaks continuously across two whole pages without allowing the young woman to insert a single remark. Had he behaved like that in reality, she would have thrown him over.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0045 }

“I do not credit it,” declared Nell plainly. Deep within her hidden spirit, she believed that the lovely, poetic statements uttered to Evadne would entirely capture the heart of any young woman. Furthermore, it was horrifying to listen to reports of Evadne, the grand, regal Evadne, “pitching” somebody. Evadne “rejected her suitors.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0046 }

“Be that as it may,” Mr. Pettifer relentlessly continued, “it is a mystery to me how Marcel Lennox failed to win her. Compared to the other, he was double the man. His actions were wicked, yet he took action. Mooning was all Perceval ever found the time to do.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0047 }

“Mooning.” The term proved to be far more disagreeable than “pitching!”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0048 }

“The bad guy was Marcel Lennox,” Nell stated with indignation. “It makes no sense to me that Perceval is less popular with everyone than he is.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0049 }

“Perceval is excessively righteous. He is infuriating. The next time you compose a story featuring a hero, include a small dash of human imperfection in his character.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0050 }

“Marcel couldn’t have been married by Evadne. Bad was what he was.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0051 }

“She would have changed him for the better. A man can be changed; naturally, a jelly-fish cannot be changed. The tale you told is not poor—I must allow that it holds some interest. However, your youth prevents you from composing a tale that would have genuine value. Allow ten years to pass.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0052 }

Nell resolved that she would not request anyone's feedback the next time she authored a tale. The process proved excessively disheartening. Even though she informed Hugh regarding the narrative, she refused to read it to him.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0053 }

“If it turns out well you will get to read it upon publication, Hugh, though if it proves a disappointment no one will ever lay eyes on it.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0054 }

Thirza was completely unaware of the project. Within her mind, Nell pictured herself reading a magazine story aloud to Thirza, tricking her into complimenting the piece—since within the imagination every outcome can occur—before victoriously revealing that she was the writer.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0055 }

Nell brought a lengthy, thick envelope to the Post Office on a certain day, directed to the absolute largest among the “big” periodicals with the charming trust typical of young, inexperienced people. Isolde felt just as much excitement about this as Nell did.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0056 }

“How much time do you think will pass prior to receiving word from it?” she inquired.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0057 }

“It ought not to take more than two weeks. Oh, I will be so delighted and filled with pride if they accept it!”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0058 }

“Naturally it is going to be accepted, and they are probable to request that you forward additional work to them. A day might come when you are as well-known as Mrs. Varley, Nell, and I will be so proud to be your acquaintance,” said Isolde, who had, if nothing else, the remarkable quality of selflessly appreciating her friends’ talents and virtues.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0059 }

Seven days of wonderful reverie ensued, after which a painful realization arrived. During a certain evening, Isolde discovered Nell inside the porch gable, her eyes appearing doubtful. Positioned upon the table were a lengthy envelope alongside a creased manuscript.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0060 }

“Nell, hasn’t your story come back?” Isolde cried in disbelief.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0061 }

“Yes, it has,” Nell answered abruptly.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0062 }

“Indeed, that editor has to be insane. What justification did he offer?”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0063 }

“There is no reason whatsoever. A printed piece of paper simply states that it was not deemed acceptable.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0064 }

“I never held a high opinion of that magazine, regardless,” Isolde stated with heat. “Its tales are not nearly as captivating as the ones in the Canadian Woman, despite its significantly higher price. I imagine the editor holds a bias against anyone who is not a Yankee. Do not lose heart, Nell. Recall how the stories of Mrs. Varley were returned. Submit yours to the Canadian Woman.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0065 }

“I think I shall,” Nell said, taking courage. “And I will mail a marked issue to that editor from America if it gets printed. However, I am going to remove the sunset. Mr. Pettifer was correct, I believe.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0066 }

The sunset came out; nevertheless, despite this valiant cutting, the Canadian Woman’s editor returned Evadne’s Atonement with such speed that an angry Isolde insisted it had not been read whatsoever, swearing she would cancel her subscription at once. Nell received this second refusal with the composure that accompanies hopelessness. She placed the manuscript under lock and key inside the attic trunk containing the former Story Club stories; however, she initially acceded to Isolde’s pleas and provided her with a duplicate.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0067 }

“My literary ambitions have come to an end,” she declared with bitterness.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0068 }

Although she never brought up the subject with Mr. Pettifer, he directly inquired of her one evening whether her story had been accepted.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0069 }

“No, the editor wouldn’t accept it,” she replied laconically.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0070 }

Mr. Pettifer glanced laterally toward the reddened, frail side of the face.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0071 }

“Well, I imagine you will continue to write them,” he remarked in a supportive tone.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0072 }

“No, I shall never try to write a story again,” announced Nell, exhibiting the despairing decisiveness of a nineteen-year-old facing a closed door.
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0073 }

“I wouldn’t throw in the towel completely,” Mr. Pettifer said musingly. “I’d compose a story every now and then, but I wouldn’t bother editors with it. I’d write about people and places such as I was familiar with, and I’d have my characters speak ordinary English; and I’d permit the sun to rise and set in the customary tranquil manner without making a big deal out of the occurrence. If it was necessary for me to include villains, I’d afford them an opportunity, Nell—I’d afford them an opportunity. I guess there exist some awfully wicked men in the world, but you’d need to travel a great distance to locate them—even if Mrs. Sowerby thinks we are all wicked. However, the majority of us possess a bit of goodness somewhere inside. Continue writing, Nell.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0074 }

“No. Attempting it was a big mistake on my part. Once my time at Wexcombe is finished, I will confine myself to teaching. Teaching is something I can do. Writing stories is not.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0075 }

“Once you have finished Wexcombe, it will be time for you to find a husband,” Mr. Pettifer said. “I do not believe in delaying marriage for too long—as I did.”
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0076 }

Nell stood up and walked briskly back to her house. Mr. Pettifer was truly unbearable on certain occasions. “Pitching,” “mooning,” and “getting a husband.” Ow!!
{: #nw-v03-c12-p0077 }
